lesson.title: From Neutral to Meaningful: The Conditioned Stimulus
lesson.summary: A conditioned stimulus is a previously neutral stimulus that, through repeated pairing with an unconditioned stimulus, comes to trigger a learned response on its own.
lesson.body:
Before conditioning begins, a stimulus like Pavlov's bell is neutral, it produces no salivation and carries no particular meaning related to feeding. What turns it into something meaningful is repetition: pairing the neutral stimulus with the unconditioned stimulus, generally with the neutral stimulus occurring just before or alongside the unconditioned stimulus, across a number of trials. This repeated pairing process is called acquisition, and it is where learning actually happens.

Timing matters a good deal in how reliably this learning takes place. Conditioning tends to be strongest when the neutral stimulus reliably predicts the unconditioned stimulus, appearing shortly before it in a consistent, repeatable pattern, rather than appearing randomly or well after the fact. Once the association is well learned, the formerly neutral stimulus has become a conditioned stimulus, and it can now trigger a response on its own, even in the complete absence of the original unconditioned stimulus.

A conditioned stimulus only keeps its power because of its track record. If it starts appearing repeatedly without the unconditioned stimulus following it, the learned response tends to fade over time, a related process called extinction. This is a useful thing to notice outside the laboratory too. A notification sound that has been repeatedly paired with stressful messages can come to trigger a jolt of anxiety on its own, functioning much like a conditioned stimulus, even though nothing about the sound itself is inherently stressful.
